extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations, public affairs, and government relations (corporate communications managers, policy/advocacy staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and running corporate public affairs/government relations programs, including Washington/state relations, PACs, grassroots lobbying, advocacy advertising, issues and stakeholder management, and involvement of management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Washington representative communication activities
rubrics_metrics.description: In carrying out these relations, Washington representatives engage in five kinds of communication activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The five activities are: Fact-finding, Liaison, Interpretation of Government Action to Management, Information Giving, and Advocacy. These are the basic functions a Washington rep performs to keep the organization informed, maintain contacts, explain legislation/regulation and analyze implications, provide data to government, and recommend/pursue persuasive action (lobbying, grassroots campaigns, communication campaigns). Includes example behaviors like setting up a news-bureau-style beat, attending hearings, bringing in experts to testify, and registering as lobbyists when influencing legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-finding (Washington reps)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most basic aspect of the Washington rep’s job provides the organization with advance information on what government policies or rules are in the making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods include setting up a news-bureau-like operation, covering beats (Congress, agencies), gathering information, and communicating it inside the organization via newsletters (Exhibit 14-1). Purpose is advance warning and intelligence for planning public affairs responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liaison (Washington reps)
rubrics_metrics.description: The representative makes personal contacts to exchange information with government officials, reporters, members of professional societies, or scientists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes attending hearings, interviewing officials, calling on congressional and agency staff, talking with trade association executives, and entertaining. Emphasizes personal relationship-building as a communications function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of government action to management
rubrics_metrics.description: Once representatives have gathered facts and maintained liaison, they interpret the results to management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They explain legislation, regulation, or rulings and analyze what actions might be necessary — translating technical/policy developments into managerial implications and recommended responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information giving (to government)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information also flows from Washington representatives to government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reps provide statistical or market data and explain the effect proposed legislation/rules might have on their organization — serving as sources of information for policymakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy (Washington reps)
rubrics_metrics.description: If fact-finding or liaison shows that the organization should take action, the representative recommends and/or implements advocacy (lobbying, grassroots campaigns, communication campaigns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Washington reps may function as lobbyists (must register if they spend majority time influencing legislation) or coordinate persuasive efforts of others, bring in experts/execs to testify, and execute advocacy tactics described in Chapter 33 (lobbying techniques).

rubrics_metrics.name: State relations program — one-state companies
rubrics_metrics.description: One-state companies can develop a full-fledged state relations program similar to federal-level programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Components include: professional lobbyists on staff in the state capital; managers who cultivate relationships with local legislators; hiring legal or public affairs consultants; coordination with trade associations (especially state Chamber of Commerce); seeking support of 'satellite groups' (suppliers/customers/unions); and direct appeals to the public to influence the legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: State relations program — multistate companies
rubrics_metrics.description: Multistate companies concentrate resources regionally and cannot have full programs in every state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical practices: concentrate on headquarters state and influential states; regionalize with specialists for groups of states; supplement with trade associations, consultants, and local managers to carry out state relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political Action Committee (PAC) basic requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A PAC must have a chairman and treasurer and is governed by federal law about contribution and solicitation practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top corporate officers rarely serve as PAC officers; government relations, public affairs, finance, and legal personnel are usually represented. Laws (Federal Election Campaign Practices Act and amendments) shaped PAC formation and regulation. Organizations can use general funds to administer PACs; individuals can donate up to $5,000 to a PAC per election cycle; a PAC can donate no more than $5,000 to a single candidate in a single federal election. Rules prohibit coercing members/employees to give money to a PAC.

rubrics_metrics.name: PAC solicitation devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices corporations use to solicit PAC contributions from employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common devices include letters from the CEO or PAC chairman, individual contacts, solicitation meetings, solicitation brochures, and management newsletters. Survey evidence (Conference Board study) shows these are frequently used.

rubrics_metrics.name: PAC usage pattern and impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Which organizations have PACs and how PACs function in political influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More regulated industries and industries that are congressional targets are more likely to have PACs (railroads, utilities, oil, banks, drug companies, aerospace contractors). PACs are often intended to 'open doors' rather than directly influence elections; business PACs generally give to both parties and to challengers as well as incumbents; PACs function best as part of a two-way symmetric public affairs program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grassroots lobbying — target constituencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporations mobilize support from publics at the grassroots level who share common interests with the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: According to Conference Board study, the most common corporate grassroots constituencies (in order) are: employees, stockholders, plant communities, retirees, and labor unions. Corporations set up systems to ask these groups to write/call/visit legislators or otherwise support corporate positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal grassroots network systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalized systems companies establish to mobilize grassroots constituents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two examples: government key contact program (select employees who understand company and political process and live in the targeted legislator's district) and the congressional district identification system (identify key constituents, enter names into a computerized system for quick contact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications on political issues — tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporations use media relations and advocacy advertising to communicate positions to influential publics and the political process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics include stories on executive speeches, stories quoting government experts, 'canned' editorials, signed columns, 'economic reality' stories, responding to television programs (requests for unedited responses), and paid advocacy advertising when access is denied or uncontrolled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy advertising — benefits and risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocacy advertising is a 'two-edged instrument' that can educate the public but can backfire if used as a substitute for corporate action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sethi: best when it contributes to public understanding of realistic corporate expectations; harmful if it substitutes for positive corporate action leading to hostility and calls for more government control. Kalman's study: advocacy advertising can attract media attention and put companies on the media agenda, increasing their use as information sources; best when tied to genuine two-way symmetric engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate right of free speech (Bellotti precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court decision First National Bank of Boston v. Bellotti (1978) expanded corporate rights to speak on public issues even when not directly affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision struck down laws that prevented corporations from spending money to publicize positions on public policy issues. It affected similar state laws and made it easier for corporations to speak out on public policy, though some restrictions remain and further legal efforts may occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy messaging — framing examples
rubrics_metrics.description: How corporations frame advocacy messages instead of overtly selling products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Weyerhaeuser preaches conservation rather than selling paper; Kellogg promotes nutrition rather than cereal; Bethlehem Steel argues trade policy; AT&T celebrates technology; Citibank extols capitalism. Guidance implies framing should connect company stance to broader social values/topics rather than direct product promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public issues management — corporate response modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Four possible corporate responses to policy issues: Reactive, Accommodative, Proactive, and Interactive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reactive = fighting change; Accommodative = adapting to change; Proactive = influencing change (fits two-way asymmetric model); Interactive = adjusting to change (fits two-way symmetric model). Issues management is used to make proactive and interactive responses, with the interactive/symmetric response seen as most effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issues-management process steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical flowchart/sequence for issues-management programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps include: Identifying public issues and trends in public expectations; Creating a list of issues of interest; Evaluating their impact and setting priorities; Research and analysis; Position development and position options; Recommended position and choice; Strategy development and choice of strategies; Implementation (tactics, alliances, communication); Evaluation and assessment of results. Corporations (ALCOA, IBM examples) staff issue centers and assign issue managers to research and develop strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder management
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholder management identifies publics who have a stake in an issue, assesses their potential for cooperation or competition, and develops strategies for dealing with each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders are groups whose collective behavior can directly affect the organization's future but are not under its control. Stakeholder management ties publics into the public affairs process, goes beyond issues management by identifying key publics, and stresses bargaining/negotiation; it works best with a two-way symmetric model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community relations (public affairs component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Community relations as part of public affairs emphasizes community participation projects, philanthropy, and contacts with local political leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors argue community relations should be managed as a separate program from public affairs and include activities beyond public affairs. Public affairs component tends to emphasize participation, philanthropy, and political contacts rather than broader community relations tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involving management in public affairs — training and assignment practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods companies use to train and involve managers in public affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices include: providing courses/seminars/workshops; bringing in outside experts; introducing new media (newsletters); rotating or assigning managers to jobs that develop public affairs competence; approving assignments outside company related to public affairs; assigning managers to standing/special committees/task forces; giving managers special assignments with public affairs content; including public affairs responsibilities in performance appraisals and compensation; encouraging self-development (reading); and encouraging voluntary participation in public affairs/community activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public affairs publics — three primary types
rubrics_metrics.description: Public affairs programs are generally designed for three kinds of publics: Active constituent publics, Activist publics, and Governmental publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active constituent publics recognize the same problems and perceive involvement; Activist publics object to organizational consequences and bring complaints to the policy arena; Governmental publics include legislators, regulators, and executive-branch officials who formulate and enforce policy. Targeting and strategy differ by public type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grunig situational model categories of publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Four types of publics that emerge from issues: active on all issues, apathetic on all issues, active only on issues that involve nearly everyone, and single-issue publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public affairs specialists should expect constituent and activist publics to fall into 'all-issues' or 'single-issue' publics; apathetic publics are not primary targets except when issues arise that engage them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publics from corporate responsibility issues — aware/activist/passive typology
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical identification of three publics from a study of corporate responsibility issues: an 'aware public', an 'activist public', and a 'passive public'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aware public: high involvement/problem recognition on secondary responsibilities, high constraint recognition (likely to seek government help); Activist public: high involvement/problem recognition on many issues and high constraint recognition — likely to join pressure groups and demand change; Passive public: low involvement/problem recognition except for widely involving issues — pay attention when such issues arise. Use these distinctions to shape communications: corrective communications for aware publics, advocacy/engagement for activist publics, monitoring and targeted outreach for passive publics.
